25_marg575: Morally. By Job is meant Christ, that is, the head and the body; so after the history, having seen from the head what we are to believe, let us see from the body what we are to hold in living. Job in the land of Hus, that is, ‘grieving’ in ‘counsel’: he who does not consider the things above exults in these things as though they were good; but he who attends to the eternal things he has lost grieves, and finds counsel to despise these; and the more the knowledge of counsel grows to forsake these, the more grows the grief that he does not yet reach the eternal. Whence Solomon: “he that addeth knowledge, addeth also labour,” because he who knows the highest things which he does not have grieves the more over these lowest. But he who seeks the eternal is simple in work, not double like one who seeks praise from good deeds. Whence Isaias: “Woe to the sinner that goeth on the earth two ways,” as when the work is God’s and the intention the world’s. Upright in faith in the highest things which he perceives within; this he begins from fear but completes by charity. Whence: “fearing God and avoiding evil”: when charity follows fear, he fully avoids evil who out of love of God begins to be unwilling to sin, not he who does so from fear. For he sins in what he would do if he could do it unpunished; because by fear vice is held down, by charity the virtues spring up. Whence he adds: “And there were born sons.” When the Spirit makes the mind fruitful, seven virtues are born in it: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, the fear of God. But these sons have three sisters, when whatever they do they join to faith, hope and charity, without which one does not come to the perfection of ten. These virtues are followed by every kind of thought of good works. Whence he adds: “And his possession was.” We possess seven thousand sheep when we feed our innocent thoughts within us, in perfect purity of heart, with the pasture of truth sought out. We possess three thousand camels when whatever is lofty and crooked in us we bow down to humility under the knowledge of the Trinity, so that bearing one another’s burdens we may have compassion on our brother’s weakness. Or the camels are the good management of earthly things, in which there is something of God and something of the world, though done for eternal things; yet they are not without disturbance of the mind. With the head, by chewing the cud, they agree with the law, because by managing these well they seek heavenly things; with their feet they creep, because what they do is of the world; they do not divide the hoof, because they do not lift themselves wholly from earthly things. So when we subject our earthly occupations to the knowledge of the Trinity, we possess camels, as it were, by faith. The yoke of oxen: virtues in concord, ploughing up the hardness of the heart. We possess she asses when we hold down wanton motions, or when within us we govern simple thoughts, which are slow and do not run among subtler things, but bear the brothers’ burdens the more gently, and humble themselves to outward works; of both there are five hundred. For whether in what we wisely understand or in what we humbly do not know, while we seek eternal rest we are held within the number of the jubilee.
25_marg576: Allegorically. Job, ‘grieving’, that is, Christ, who carried our sorrows. Hus, ‘counsellor’. So he dwells in the land of Hus, that is, in hearts given to the counsels of life. Whence: “I wisdom dwell in counsel.” Simple and upright: we forsake gentleness for justice, and justice for gentleness; but Christ as man kept both fully, fearing God. Whence: “And he shall be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord.” He also avoided evil, not that by doing it he touched it, but that finding it in the world he condemned it. Seven sons: by this number perfection is signified. The sons, the strong apostles; the daughters, the weak faithful; or those who hold the faith of the Trinity; or, after the strong apostles, three daughters, that is, the three orders of the faithful in the Church, pastors, the continent and the married, that is, Noe, Daniel and Job. What is said generally of the daughters is said distinctly of the animals. Seven thousand sheep: the perfect innocence of those who came to grace from the pastures of the law. Three thousand camels: the whole gentile world coming to the fulness of faith; or the Samaritans, who chew the cud in that they receive the law in part, but do not divide the hoof, because in part they despise it; and of these the Lord brought many to faith, as he did the Hebrews. The oxen: workers of the faith. The asses: the simplicity of the gentiles, on which the Lord sits as he goes to Jerusalem, that is, leading them to the vision of peace. Of both it is said: “The ox knoweth” (that is, the Jew, pressed by the yoke of the law) “his owner” (that is, God, whom he worshipped but did not know), “and the ass” (that is, the brutish gentile, driven where the seducer willed) “his master’s crib” (that is, the fodder of the law). So what he said above of the sheep and camels he repeats in the oxen and asses. Five hundred: this number is made of fifty taken ten times; fifty signifies rest, ten perfection; because to the faithful of both peoples the perfection of rest is promised.
25_marg577: Allegorically. The household is put after the animals, because first he chose the foolish things of the world, so that not eloquence but the cause itself might persuade to the faith; afterwards the shrewd too were gathered in.
25_marg578: Simple and upright and fearing God, etc. The person is described as fit before his battle is told, so that such a man may be seen able to conquer.
25_marg579: Simple: the simplicity of the dove must be instructed by the wisdom of the serpent, and the serpent’s wisdom tempered by simplicity. Hence the Spirit appeared in a dove and in fire, because those who are full of him so serve the gentleness of simplicity that they are kindled against evils by the zeal of uprightness.
25_interl1863: to fear God is to pass over nothing that ought to be done
25_marg580: Fearing God: Solomon: “he that feareth God, neglecteth nothing.” Avoiding evil: Solomon again: “he that shall offend in one, shall lose many good things.”
25_marg581: The animals are called legal, that is, clean according to the law, which both chew the cud and divide the hoof; the camels have the one but lack the other, and so they agree with the law and disagree. 25_marg582: A family exceeding great: the countless crowd of thoughts, which, like maidservants when the mistress, that is, reason, is away, leave their work and make a din; but when she returns they work in silence. If we rule these well, the mind is not overcome by their number.

25_marg583: Among all the people of the east: that is, among the angels who cleave to the light of the east; we are great when we are their companions.
25_marg584: The people of the east are all who are in Christ by faith, of whom the prophet says: “the Orient is his name”; all these the God-man surpasses.
25_marg585: Allegorically. His sons went: that is, the apostles throughout the world, serving the banquets of the word of God, each in his day, that is, according to the measure of his enlightened understanding. The sisters, that is, the weaker, are refreshed by Scripture, which in its obscure places is food, broken by exposition, and in its plain places is drink, swallowed as it is.
25_interl1871: great wealth breeds discord among brothers; but the father so trained them that, though they would divide their father’s goods, they were of one mind
25_marg586: Morally. The sons make feasts, because each virtue feeds the mind after its own manner. In his day, because each virtue has its own enlightenment: wisdom has one day, understanding another, and so the rest. Many have a taste of eternal things but cannot understand them. Wisdom therefore feeds in its day when it refreshes the mind with the hope and certainty of eternal things; understanding in its day, when it enlightens the heart about what it has heard; counsel in its day, when it fills the reason and forbids it to be headlong; fortitude in its day, when it gives the fearful confidence against adversity; knowledge drives out ignorance; piety teaches works of mercy; the fear of the Lord holds the mind down lest it be proud of present things, and strengthens it with the hope of things to come. They feed one another, because one supports another, and without that each is badly destitute. Wisdom is less if it lacks understanding; understanding is useless without wisdom, for if without it it penetrates higher things, its own lightness lifts it up to fall more heavily. Counsel is worthless without fortitude, because what it finds by deliberation it cannot bring to act without strength. Fortitude, which can do more, rushes headlong without the restraint of reason. Knowledge is nothing without piety, because he who does not carry out the good he knows is judged more heavily. Piety without the discernment of knowledge does not know how to have mercy. Fear without the others avails nothing, because, trembling at everything, it is numb to good works.
25_marg587: The three sisters, that is, faith, hope and charity, the virtues call into all that they do, that they may rejoice in it; they gain strength as from food when they become more confident through good works; they are inebriated as with drink after food when they long to be steeped in the dew of contemplation. But from these very goods evils also arise, such as pride, or when the mind takes delight in them; and a certain security comes too, and from it torpor. So he adds: “And when the days were gone about.” To sanctify the sons when the feast is over is, after the exercise of the virtues, to direct the intention of the heart, and to cleanse all that is done by strict reconsideration, lest one be deceived by the quality of evil, so that things which are evil are thought good; or by the quantity of good, so that it is believed sufficient when it is not perfect. But this he finds better by praying than by examining; for the mind raised up by compunction judges more surely everything beneath it. Whence he says: “And rising up early.” He rises early who, flooded with the light of compunction, leaves the human night and opens his eyes to the true light. He offers for each when he offers prayers to God for each virtue: lest wisdom exalt, lest understanding stray, lest counsel confuse by multiplying itself, lest fortitude through confidence throw headlong, lest knowledge puff up, lest piety turn aside from what is right, lest fear, trembling more than is just, despair.
25_marg588: Mystically, by houses: as Peter through Rome, Philip in Samaria. In his day, that is, according to the measure of his understanding; for Paul taught in one way among the Greeks, Peter in another among the Romans, though they did not disagree in faith.
25_marg589: Allegorically. And when … were gone about: the days of the feast go about when the mysteries of the preaching are completed; when all is done, Job offers for his sons, because Christ prayed to the Father for the apostles returning from preaching, and by sending the Holy Spirit sanctified them, cleansing whatever fault could be in them.
25_marg590: He rises early to offer, because as he prays for them he scatters the night and enlightens their minds, lest they be defiled in secret by any taint of sin from their preaching by ascribing it to themselves. Whence he adds: “Lest perhaps my sons have sinned, and have blessed,” that is, cursed, “God.” To curse God is to give oneself glory for his gift. Hence also after the preaching the Lord washed the apostles’ feet, because in a good work the dust of sin is gathered, such as inward pride, which the Lord wipes away. “Perhaps” is said, not that he does not know all things, but from our doubting, as: “shall he find, think you, faith on earth?” “So did Job all days,” because he always offers for us, while he shows the Father on our behalf his incarnation, by which he washes away sins.
25_marg591: When the days of the feast were gone about: because after the seven brothers had finished their feasts, Job is said to offer seven sacrifices. For it is plain that he does this on the eighth day, on which one full of the sevenfold Spirit is shown serving the Lord in hope of the resurrection.
25_interl1872: what he would do when present, when even absent his care is not lacking
25_interl1873: because he knows that feasts can hardly be held without fault, for pleasure and talkativeness almost always attend banquets
25_marg592: Offered holocausts: a holocaust means wholly burnt; that is when the whole mind is kindled with the fire of compunction on the altar of love, and burns up the defilements of thought as of its offspring; which none knows how to do but he who, before thought passes into deed, bridles his inner motions, and guards his mind with a manly watch, not a womanish one like Isboseth’s. Whence Solomon: “With all watchfulness keep thy heart, because life issueth out from it.” For the virtues, that is, the good things we do, are weighed by the source of the intention. For he said: “Lest perhaps they have sinned and blessed,” that is, cursed, “in their hearts.” He curses in his heart who does right works with no right intention, who thinks he has of himself what he is, or, if he has it from God, seeks his own praise from it. The things that are good before men the devil defiles in three ways.
25_marg593: First he corrupts the intention of a good work, so that one does good for the favour of men. Whence the prophet: “Her adversaries are become her lords” (Lamentations: literally “in the head”), that is, they rule at the beginning of the thought. If he cannot do this, if the good is well begun, he sets himself more secretly against it in the doing, as on the road; as though to kill one going securely, he puts praise in the way, which, though not sought, delights when offered; or anger, which in zeal for what is right troubles the mind too immoderately; or sadness, or immoderate gladness. Whence David: “In this way wherein I walked, they have hidden a snare for me.” But if he neither corrupts the beginning nor trips one up on the road, as though driven off he lies in wait more craftily at the end. Whence: “they will watch my heel”; and the serpent, if its head, that is, the beginning of its suggestion, is caught, lies in wait for the heel, that is, it strives to deceive at the end. In all things, then, each ought to look about him and persevere in this. Whence: “So did Job all days,” that the tunic may cover the ankle, that is, that good action may cover us before the eyes of God to the end of life.

25_marg594: On a certain day: at the beginning, the quality and the end of a thing are expressed; so now Job’s temptation is said to begin from a day, because he is led to victory; and so in other places. Now a thing is signified by the quality of the time, as that the angels appear to Abraham at midday, and Judas goes out by night; now by the place, as that Israel, being weak, hears the law not on the mountain but below; now by the quality of the air, as when it is said “it was winter” when he preaches to those who will not believe, and “it was cold” as Peter’s denial drew near; now by the position of the body, as that Stephen saw Jesus standing.
25_marg595: Allegorically. Nothing is said to be done before the Lord “on a certain day” because there is change of time with him; but he uses our words in condescension, so that while he speaks of the eternal in temporal terms he may raise our minds, accustomed to temporal things, to the eternal. Or Satan was present “on a certain day” because God saw darkness in light; and he who sees all things, good and evil, at once is not diverse in the things he orders in diverse order, nor is his light darkened by the presence of darkness. Satan was among the sons of God because he is pierced by the very force of justice with which the good spirits are filled; he is transfixed by the ray with which they are flooded that they may shine. Among the sons of God, because, although in a different way, he still serves God. Whence in the book of Kings: “I saw the Lord sitting on his throne” (that is, upon the angels, over whose minds he presides on high and orders all things below) “and all the army of heaven standing by him on the right hand and on the left,” that is, good and evil angels; because not only the good angels serve God but also the evil, who try men and weigh down those who wish to be converted. Of these a lying spirit springs forward into the midst, by whom King Achab, as his deserts required, is deceived.

25_marg596: Mystically. On the day the Lord saw Satan, because by his incarnation he rebuked the ways of his folly, which he had, as it were, not seen when for so long he had borne his wickedness in the ruin of men. “Whence comest thou?” Because by his coming he laid bare his ways and, holding them in check, rebuked them. On this day the sons of God stand before God, because then, called to their homeland, they already stand before the Godhead by his foreknowledge. “I have gone round about the earth and walked through it,” because he had pressed his footprints into the hearts of the gentiles and gone round as though by right, because he found none who resisted him fully; but now he is held down by him who in the flesh is without sin, whose astounding pride and fearful weakness is set before him by God. “Hast thou considered?” For on earth there is none like him, because the others are adopted by grace, he is God by nature, though in the form of a servant. For the Lord to say this is to declare to the proud one what he should wonder at and grieve to consider; to curb his pride he lists that man’s virtues. Simple and upright Christ came, to give men an example of life: simple, that he might not yield to evil spirits; upright, to overthrow pride; fearing God, to wipe away the uncleanness of life, avoiding evil.
25_marg597: They too were sent from their ministries, confined in place, where yet they always stand by and “see the face of the Father.” So they go out to us by their ministry, yet by spiritual presence and inward contemplation they are always with God.
25_marg598: Because although by pride he went out, yet he did not lose a nature like theirs; so he was present among them, because God, with the gaze by which he beholds all spiritual things, sees Satan too in the order of the higher nature; yet Satan does not see God, who is seen by the clean of heart, as a blind man does not see the light by which he is shone upon.
25_marg599: And the Lord said to him: the Lord and Satan do not converse by the breath of the voice, since they are bodiless, as we do, who stand in the secret of the heart as though behind the wall of the body until we come out through the tongue. Nor is the speech of a bodiless nature of one kind. God speaks to the angels when his will is breathed into them. The angels speak to God when they marvel at what is above them, to the praise of God; their loud voice in the ears of God is their wonder at God’s power in praising him. Holy souls speak to God by their desires, which do not disagree with God; not that they do not know what is to come, but the more ardently they cleave to him, the more they receive from him to ask of him what they see he wills to do; and if they did not ask, they would be out of accord with his will; and God answers them when by his foreknowledge he strengthens them amid their desires with the certainty of the reward. But God speaks to the devil in four ways. He reproves his ways, as “Whence comest thou?” He sets the justice of his elect against him, as “Hast thou considered my servant Job?”; which is to make them such that he may envy them. He allows him to tempt innocence, as “All that he hath is in thy hand”; which is to let loose his malice against the faithful for their proving. Sometimes he forbids him to dare to tempt, as “Put not forth thy hand upon him”; which is to restrain him from the onset of immoderate temptation. The devil speaks to God in three ways. He tells his ways, as “I have gone round about the earth”: to say what he has done is to know that he cannot hide his acts from him. He accuses the innocent with feigned crimes, as “Doth Job fear God in vain?”; which is to complain against the good and envy their progress, and to seek chinks for doing harm. He asks that innocence be tempted, as “Stretch forth thy hand”; which is to pant with the heat of his malice for the affliction of the good.
25_marg600: Whence comest thou? He does not ask of the good, because we ask only what we do not know; and for God not to know is to reject; as a good man too is said not to know how to lie, not because he does not know, but because he despises it. So to say “Whence comest thou?” is to reject his ways as though unknown. “I have gone round about the earth”: by the circling round, the anxiety of toil is signified. He goes about the earth toiling who did not stand at rest in heaven; and he does not fly over it but walks through it, because he has fallen from the flight of spiritual power, weighed down by the heaviness of his own malice. Of his members also it is said: “The wicked walk round about,” that is, they are wearied in toil over outward things.
25_marg601: The devil strives not against Job, but against God, with Job in between. Hence Job was not first asked of God; but God praised him in his sight.
25_marg602: Morally. Satan among the sons of God, because he thrusts himself among the good thoughts that are from God, to disturb them; but God uncovers him to us as he lurks. Whence it is said: “Whence comest thou?”; which is to lay open his snares to us. “I have gone round about the earth”: he searches fleshly hearts to sow evil in them; nor does he fly over but walks through, because he does not quickly leave the one he tempts, but lingers to press in the footprints of wickedness. Against him Job is praised: “Hast thou considered my servant?”: the man whom God makes good and strengthens he praises, as it were, in Satan’s hearing; whence he rages the more fiercely, saying: “Doth he fear in vain?”, as if to say: why do you praise one whom you protect? He would deserve praise if, with me disregarded, he stood against me by his own strength. Whence he maliciously asks: “But stretch forth a little.” While good things abound the mind is lifted up a little, as though its good were from itself; the devil seeks these good things wickedly, but God allows the trial for good, so that while the man is shaken in those goods, knowing his weakness, he may be made firm in God. Whence he adds: “Behold, all the substance that he hath is in thy hand.”

25_marg603: Doth … in vain, etc. Mystically. The devil had sensed that the Redeemer had come; but because of the lowly things he suffered, whatever he suspected of his Godhead came, for his pride, into doubt; and he believed him not God born, but guarded by God’s grace: “Hast not thou made a fence?” He calls the house fenced because by tempting he could not penetrate his conscience, and his substance, because he did not presume to attack his elect.
