25_marg605: His possession: as if, because he has received so many goods on earth, he behaves innocently for their sake, but he would be innocent if he stood amid adversity; because he cannot reprove him in the day, he wishes to in the night of adversity. Knowing then that not Job’s strength but every man is more truly proved by adversity, he asks that he be tempted. “But stretch forth”: he does not ascribe to himself even the power to strike; his will, which is from himself, is always wicked; his power, which is from God, is just. Whence: “an evil spirit from the Lord” upon Saul: of the Lord by leave, and evil by will.
25_marg606: Thy hand: he complains that the number of the faithful grows as the apostles preach; for Satan to say this is to think such things in envy and to grieve, wasting away, over them.
25_marg607: Touch all: because it is outward things he asks to have crushed, and he thinks it little unless he harm the soul.
25_marg608: To thy face: the face of the Lord is the regard of grace. So he says: if you take away the gifts he loves, he will not seek your regard, that is, of your grace, your favour, but will despise it with cursing.
25_marg609: Behold, all, etc. Only upon him …: that is, I grant his goods to be tempted outwardly, but within I keep him for myself.
25_marg610: Then the Lord said: God is not overcome, provoked by the devil’s request, but grants the enemy, to his grief and his deceiving, what profits his servant.
25_marg611: Behold, all that: with loving dispensation he lets loose and restrains; he gives up his substance, protects his body; and though afterwards he would give up the body, yet not everything at once, lest heaped together they should destroy what, divided, could be borne. Or the Lord knew Job was strong, and yet he divided the battles, so that he might be the more wonderful a victor when the conquered enemy readied himself again for new battles.
25_marg612: Mystically. “But stretch forth”: he thought that through sufferings Christ could sin. “Behold, all that he hath is in thy hand.” Satan’s hand is not power but temptation. First Judea, which had been his possession, was taken away by unbelief and turned against him; afterwards his flesh too was crucified.
25_marg613: Went forth: that is, he attained the wishes of his desire.
25_marg614: Or he goes forth when what is permitted him with a good intention is carried out by him with a wicked one.
25_marg615: Whither? He went out from him who is everywhere. But as long as Satan, held down by the power of God, could not carry out what he desired, he stood, as it were, before his face; he goes out when he is let loose to carry out his desire.
25_marg616: Because, while he cannot prevail as far as the heart, shut out from within he wanders outside; even if he troubles the mind, he is outside, because he does not destroy but instructs.
25_marg617: Now upon a certain day: times are suited to temptations. He chose a fit time for tempting, when he found his sons at a feast; the gladness of fulness is a forewarning of trouble.
25_marg618: Allegorically. Now upon a certain day when his sons and daughters, etc.: the apostles and all the faithful. The elder son is the Jewish people, begotten by the law; the younger, the gentiles, called at the end. So the apostles feast in the house of the firstborn, because they still fed on the delights of holy Scripture in the gathering of the Jewish people alone, to whom it was then said: “Go ye not into the way of the Gentiles.”
25_marg619: Morally. To eat is to rejoice in good works; to drink wine is to burn with heavenly desire.
25_marg620: Morally. First there is born in the heart wisdom, which is faith; for then we are wise if we believe all that the Lord says. Whence: “If you will not believe, you shall not understand.” So the other virtues are filled with the holy word in the house of faith, that is, in the mind, without which there are no good things, even if they seem good; and in the house of wisdom, because unless they do prudently what they desire they are not virtues. But when this is not done the devil takes away the oxen and asses and kills the servants. The oxen are the weightier thoughts, which by working the heart yield richer fruit; but these the enemy sometimes corrupts by slipping in the delight of pleasure. The asses feeding: the simple motions of the heart, nourished in purity, guarded from doubleness. But to these too the devil shows subtleties, so that while praise is sought from them, simplicity is lost. Or the oxen ploughing: thoughts of charity, which cut into the hearts of the hard by ploughing, that is, by preaching; but these thoughts the enemy kills through the torpor of negligence; or, if they are on their guard, he snatches something in that which prevails over thought for a moment. The asses: the gentleness of patience, for which the devil lays snares out of what it most loves, so that from there its great patience may be troubled. But the elect return to themselves and afflict themselves heavily for a slight movement; yet when he troubles patience even for a moment, he exults that he has taken the asses. In what is to be done, reason, the guardian, weighs what suits each thing; but when the enemy troubles suddenly, forestalling one’s watchfulness unexpectedly, he kills the servants, the guardians, as it were. One escapes, that is, the discernment of reason returns to the mind and announces what is lost, so that what the forestalled mind lost the afflicted mind may recover.
25_interl1898: this messenger is reason; yet each time another and another, because it announces one thing and another
25_marg621: Mystically, the oxen ploughing, that is, the good working well; the asses, those living simply; these are beside the oxen because they feed on their understanding. The Sabeans taking them captive, that is, the demons; the servants, that is, beginners, not yet of manly constancy; with the sword, that is, with despair of eternity. The messenger who escapes is the prophetic word, which says: “my people is led away captive, because they had not knowledge”; because when the evils it foretold come about, it returns, as it were, safe to the Lord; for it is known to have foretold truly the captivity of the weak.
25_interl1899: how craftily the losses are announced, so that by recalling the fruit of the work the cause of grief may grow; whence here too the Greeks read ‘she asses in foal’
25_interl1900: while we suffer outwardly we flee for comfort to divine grace; this is said to come from the Sabeans and from God, that there may be no comfort, so that, left destitute on every side, he may break out in despair into insult
25_interl1901: neighbours sometimes bring comfort, but these persecute
25_interl1902: because adversities strike harder if, when they are many, they are also announced suddenly; so the devil has them announced
25_marg622: And the servants. Morally. He calls servants that wariness of diligence by which one provides for these things, and which is struck in them too.
25_interl1904: he incites him not only by the loss of his goods but by the messengers’ words, when it is craftily said “the fire of God,” as though he were suffering his vengeance, whom he used to appease with so many victims; so that, thinking he had served in vain, he might grow proud against God
25_marg623: The fire of God, etc. Mystically. Heaven: the teachers of the law, the priests, from whom the fire of envy falls on the sheep and the servants, that is, the innocent and the weak. The servant returns safe, because the prophecy is plain to have spoken truly: “zeal hath taken hold of the unlearned people.”
25_marg624: The fire of God fell, etc. The sheep: the innocence of thoughts. Fire from heaven, that is, from the powers of the air, the flame of envy rushes in, and often kindles clean thoughts with the heat of lust; and it is the fire of God, not as doing it but as permitting it; and because by a sudden assault one’s watchfulness is overwhelmed, the guarding servants are killed. But discernment alone, that is, reason, announces the losses to the mind and calls the master, as it were, to lament.
25_marg625: The Chaldeans, etc. Mystically. The Chaldeans are interpreted ‘fierce’, that is, the persecutors of Christ; three troops, because the Pharisees, Herodians and Sadducees divided themselves to put questions to the Lord; and they drew after them the camels, that is, the crooked minds of fools, and the servants, because any who could use reason yielded to their authority; and true is the prophetic word which says: “they that held the law knew me not,” and: “The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes met together, against the Lord and against his Christ.” They struck the servants with the sword, that is, with wicked persuasion, etc.
25_marg626: The camels, etc. The camel, an animal clean in part, because it chews the cud, but in part unclean, because it does not divide the hoof, signifies the good management of earthly things, in which the enemy lies in wait in more ways; and he strikes such cares now with sluggish, now with headlong action; now he confounds them with slow or immoderate speech; almost always he weighs them down with too great a mass of thoughts. So the Chaldeans carry off the camels in three troops, that is, by unlawful work, superfluous speech and disordered thought they lay waste the pursuits of earthly management. Often the mind attends to what it owes itself and what its neighbours, and neither neglects itself through immoderate care for others nor puts others aside through care of itself; but while it does both skilfully, some cause suddenly arises that overwhelms all its watchfulness, and discernment alone brings back to the mind what it must weep for.
25_marg627: To tell thee, etc. Evils are announced, many and sudden, so that with wound inflicted on wound he may bear it impatiently; and the crafty enemy tries him not so much by the loss of things as by the order of the messages. First he announces lesser evils, then greater, at last the death of his sons, lest, once bereaved, the loss of things should seem cheap, when there were no heirs for whom to keep it. So he hears worse things step by step, that every wound may find a place in his heart.
25_marg628: Mystically, the sons and daughters, as was said, are the apostles and the people subject to them, who fed on Scripture in Judea. The wind, that is, strong temptation, bursts out from the desert, that is, from the hearts of the Jews or from unclean spirits; and shook the four corners on which the house stands: the priests, the scribes, the elders of the people, the Pharisees. The house, that is, Judea, falling in its persecution of the Lord, overwhelmed the apostles in despair. And true is the word about the persecuting people: “What is the meaning that my beloved hath wrought much wickedness in my house?”; and of the apostles: “my neighbours stood afar off”; and: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be dispersed,” etc.
25_marg629: At the feast of the elder brother Satan overwhelms the sons, because through the negligence of the elders he seeks an entrance to the death of the younger; and he gains more strength against others when he sees those who by their watch are set over others giving themselves to mirth. Not that they were given to the belly; but at feasts the good intention of the mind is less fervent and foresees less.
25_marg630: It is hiddenly said that he moved the elements against him at whose nod they were moved; though the devil, having once received power from God, can shake the elements for the purposes of his wickedness, as fire and water serve those condemned to the mines.
25_marg631: Morally. The side of the desert: the multitude of the demons, forsaken, from whom the wind, that is, strong temptation, rushes and overturns the conscience from its calm. The house of the mind stands on four corners, that is, prudence, temperance, fortitude, justice. These are the four rivers of paradise, which temper it against the heat of fleshly desires. But often through sloth prudence grows cold, and, being tired, foresees less; and often through delight in present things we refrain less from what is unlawful; often fear troubles fortitude; often some love turns the mind from the uprightness of justice; and when these are shaken the conscience is troubled. In the mind which is raised up on these four, the other virtues, the heart’s offspring as it were, feed one another; for the Spirit, which first of all shapes the mind with those four, equips it against each temptation with seven virtues: against folly with wisdom, against dullness with understanding, against rashness with counsel, against fear with fortitude, against ignorance with knowledge, against hardness with piety, against pride with fear. But while the mind enjoys this plenty securely, it presumes as though from itself, not from God; and so it is subtly withdrawn, that it may see in its weakness whence it had what it could not keep. So the seven virtues are struck by their contraries, that is, when the conscience is troubled the sons die for a time; and though they are troubled outwardly by temptation, they live within by the perseverance of the intention. The three sisters die too, because when one thinks oneself burdened beyond one’s strength one grows numb, as it were, in the love of God. While one fears too much, hope is weakened; while one is too much tormented by questions, faith is troubled; but yet the right intention keeps them alive within. So the servant, that is, the mind’s discernment, escapes, and deals with the mind so that what it had begun to lose it may keep by repentance.
25_marg632: Behold again, lest he grieve any less over human adversity, or likewise over that from above, he shows the wrath named in the air: a wind rushed in.
25_interl1905: he who stood firm before stands when all is lost, and this is Job’s rising up
25_marg633: Mystically. When the house fell and the sons were dead, that is, when Judea was lost and the apostles dead with fear, Job rose up, that is, Christ from the dead. Or he who lay patient raised up the judgment of justice against the reprobate. He rent his garment, that is, Judea, which, awaiting his coming, had clung to him; he divided it, taking some to faith and leaving others. With his head shaven: the head is the height of the priesthood, the hairs the subtlety of the sacraments; whence Ezechiel: “take thee a sharp knife … and cause it to pass over thy head, and over thy beard”; in this Christ is signified, who shaved the head, that is, took away the sacraments of the law from the Jewish priesthood, and the beard, because, forsaking the kingdom of Israel, he cut off from it the comeliness of strength. The earth is the sinful gentile world. So with his head shaven he fell to the ground, because, forsaking Judea, when he took away its sacraments from its priesthood he came to the knowledge of the gentiles. What falls comes suddenly to the bottom; whence for Christ to fall is to have come unexpectedly to the gentiles, as it is said: “the Spirit of the Lord fell upon them,” that is, came unexpectedly. He worshipped, that is, made them worship, as: “the Spirit himself asketh for us with unspeakable groanings.” But Christ also, in himself, according to the form of a servant, prayed to the Father.
25_marg634: Wonderful is God’s dispensation for keeping humility and watchfulness: for one who is secure grows slack in ease, but when tempted he wakes up. Whence: “Then Job rose up.” To sit belongs to one at rest, to rise to one who fights; then discernment too makes progress, and learns to distinguish virtues from vices more subtly. Whence he adds: “He rent his garments.” The garments are the works that cover us, lest we blush at our nakedness; when grief makes us weep over our fault, we judge them more strictly, as with an angry hand. Then too all pride and superfluity of thoughts fall from the mind, which is to fall with the head shaven, that is, with thoughts of presumption held down, to feel how weak one is in oneself. It is hard to do great things and not to have confidence in oneself about great things; and thoughts are the henchmen of this pride, as of a tyranny. The Nazarites let their hair grow, as through continence of life thoughts of presumption grow; when their vow is fulfilled they are commanded to shave the head and put the hair into the fire of the sacrifice, because one comes to perfection when he so overcomes outward vices as also to cut away superfluous thoughts from his mind, which he burns with the fire of divine love, so that the whole heart, burning in the love of God, may consume them in the perfection of devotion.
25_interl1907: see, he felt the pain of the scourge
25_marg635: And having shaven his head. Mystically. It is thought great constancy if one does not feel evils; others, feeling them too much, grieve without measure; but virtue is in the middle; insensibility of heart is not virtue, as limbs that are numb do not feel pain when cut. Whence the prophet: “Thou hast struck them, and they have not grieved.” Lest he break off love of neighbour, he spent mourning on his sons; lest he forsake love of God, he prayed amid his groans. Lest he be proud, not feeling it, he fell down; lest he be estranged, he worshipped the one who struck him. It was the custom of the ancients that those who kept the comeliness of their body by letting their hair grow cut it off in time of affliction, and conversely those who had cut it in time of peace let it grow as a show of affliction. So Job is shown to have kept his hair, since he cut it for the purpose of grief; so that while the hand from above struck him in everything, he might of his own will also darken himself with the various signs of penance, and show that he consented to the divine power.
25_marg636: Falling down he worshipped, because he offers true prayer who humbly sees that he is dust. Whence he also says: “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb.” Naked in faith first grace brought us forth; naked the same receives us. When, buffeted by vices, one flees naked as it were to mercy, and, being sometimes stripped of some virtue, is better clothed by humility itself, ascribing what he has not to himself but to God: “the Lord gave” the good things, and his power also takes them away; which is done for a time so that the humble man may have them better.
25_interl1909: see, in his grief he did not go too far against the judgment of the one who scourged him, but prays
25_marg637: The earth brought me forth naked as I came in here; the earth will receive me naked as I go out from here. He takes comfort from the condition of things, that he has not lost what was his own but recalls what he received and must leave; he foresees the time when he did not yet have these things, how he will go out. He comforts himself also by the justice of God.
25_interl1910: the mother is the earth, which brought forth all
25_marg638: Mystically. The mother of Christ is the Synagogue, which held him in itself covered by the letter, and did not see him naked in his Godhead; but from her he came naked to the gentiles. See Joseph, whom the Synagogue, believing him a mere man, tried to hold fast in an adulterous embrace; he left her the covering of the letter and showed himself plainly to the gentiles. But naked shall he return when at the end of the world God will make himself known to the remnant of Israel. “The Lord gave”: to Judea, when she believed he would come; “hath taken away,” when she despised him coming.
25_interl1911: not the devil; for he knows that nothing is permitted him unless God allows; so what wonder if he who gave took back his own?
25_interl1913: he teaches us to give thanks amid scourges, as he himself, drawing near to his passion, gave thanks
25_marg639: the last comfort: he knows that God is the judge here; hence he knows that nothing but what is just pleases him
25_marg640: As it hath pleased the Lord. Morally. When we are troubled we ought to run back to the judgment of God and render greater praise, because when buffeted we know ourselves more truly.
25_marg641: In a matter that displeases, it is a great comfort if it is done by the ordering of him to whom nothing pleases but what is just; why then murmur at a just thing? As though, after stating his case against his adversary, at the end of his speech he blesses the judge: “blessed be the name of the Lord.” What he felt was right he concluded with the blessing of the Lord; whence the devil blushes, who even in bliss was contumacious toward God, while man, even when struck, sings him a hymn. So Job conquers the proud enemy by humility, the cruel one by patience, and inflicted sharper wounds than he received.
25_interl1914: because even by not speaking we can sin in thought
25_marg642: In all these things … sinned not. Morally. The grieving mind guards itself lest it murmur at the fire that tries it. What was said of the virtues may be taken of those things which are given for a show of virtue, the gifts of the Spirit: prophecy, tongues, healings, which are also withdrawn lest the mind be lifted up. For the spirit of prophecy was not always in the prophets. Whence Eliseus says: “the Lord hath hid it from me.” And Amos: “I am not a prophet,” because that was then true; but the Spirit fills me when humble. And he says: “And now hear thou the word of the Lord.” Whence in the gospel: “He upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending, and remaining upon him, he it is that baptizeth.” For in others he comes, but in Christ alone he singularly remains. But how is this his sign, when he himself says of the apostles: “he shall abide with you”? But in Christ he always remains by substance for all things; in the elect by grace, not for all things. For there are some gifts of the Spirit without which one does not come to life, such as humility, faith and so on, according to which the Spirit always remains; others by which holiness of life is declared for the benefit of others, such as prophecy, healing, tongues, according to which the Spirit does not always remain, but sometimes withdraws himself from the showing of signs, so that he may be held more humbly. So concerning those that are for life let us fear lest they perish; concerning those for show, when they are sometimes withdrawn without danger, let humility comfort itself, saying: “The Lord gave”; because we show that we had them rightly when we bear their removal with an even mind.
25_marg643: Whence: “Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth.” Testimony is borne to Job both of mouth and of heart: in heart he did not swell, he did not murmur; in tongue he was not contumacious.
25_interl1915: he speaks foolishly against God who amid scourges says he is innocent; which is proudly to accuse the justice of God who strikes
25_interl1916: the same day as before, historically and mystically
25_interl1917: so that he might be seen by God, not see God himself, because he is unclean of heart
25_marg644: This is not as before; for since it is known that he has returned from the war to which he had been let loose, it is nothing else than that the weakness of his pride is rebuked, as if to say: you who raise yourself against God are conquered from below and by weak flesh. Hence, listing Job’s goods with triumph, he adds “and still keeping his innocence,” as if to say: you have exercised your malice, but he keeps his innocence, and you who wished to lessen him have served his progress.
25_marg645: Innocence, etc. Morally. He keeps innocence who even after a fall, stirred by a spark of reason, faithfully repents.
25_interl1918: not that God is stirred up, but in our way of speaking, who do not strike unless moved; God’s very striking is called being moved
25_marg646: Allegorically. How was the Father, with whom he is one, moved against Christ by Satan? Because Christ as man would not have suffered had Adam not sinned; when Satan moved Adam he moved God against Christ. “Without cause,” because he bore the punishment without fault of his own; but not without cause, because he paid what another had stolen.
25_interl1919: not without cause, because the virtue of patience and glory grew in him, and what lay hidden in him was shown to us as wonderful; but without cause, because in him sin is not punished; or without cause, that is, it did not come about as you hoped
25_marg647: The devil, from the miracles, thought him the Son of God, but from the lowly things, a mere man. So, judging him by others who, instead of shepherds, think little of others’ losses, as though unmoved by the many things taken away, since they are outside him, he tempts him with the pain of his own flesh, as though he would grieve for himself who did not for others. When he asks for this to be done, he says it with his desires. These things he also brought on him through his members, by words and desires, through whom he said: “Let us put wood on his bread,” that is, let us apply the stock of the cross to his body by fastening it there.
25_marg648: Skin is given for skin, because often when a blow comes at the eye we put up a hand, so as to be wounded in it rather than in the more tender part; knowing this to be the usual way, he says: “Skin for skin, and all that a man hath,” as if Job bears so many scourges outside himself with an even mind because he dreads being struck himself, and through care for himself feels less for his own; whence he asks that he himself be struck: “Put forth thy hand”; which God rightly permits, so that, often defeated, he may be silenced.
25_interl1922: that is, whatever, one by one, all
25_interl1923: he will lay it out without grief, provided only that he keep his life safe
25_interl1924: this the devil suspected of Job, which he often saw in others
25_interl1925: that is, if you do not believe that he bears outward things patiently for this reason: whoever fears for his life loves something. Let me loose on his life and you will see
25_marg649: But put forth thy hand. Morally. Often the devil, after he has assailed the mind, stops for a time, so as to burst in suddenly on it when secure; so he asks for Job again, whom God, by keeping him, grants him.
25_marg650: Touch his bone and his flesh. Morally. By the bone and the flesh he understands the bodily life; by the soul, reason, as above.
25_marg651: Allegorically. Satan had power through his own over the flesh of Christ, but keeps his soul, not that he does not tempt it, but that he does not overcome it. Or “the soul,” that is, the dear and elect, he loses from his right when he kills him; “from the sole of the foot to the top of the head,” because from the beginning of the world he brought hard things on his members, and in his raging reached even their head, that is, Christ.
25_marg652: Behold he is in thy hand, etc. He allows us to be tempted, that we may see ourselves weak; and yet he guards us.
25_marg653: Went forth, etc. Morally. Having received leave, from the sole, that is, from the least things, coming to greater, he tears the whole body of the mind with the temptations he brings, but does not reach the soul; because among the delights it undergoes the intention resists, and the deliberation of what is right is not bent to the softness of consent. Yet those delights too must be wiped away by the harshness of penance, which is to scrape the corrupt matter with a potsherd. For the potsherd is the rigour of strictness, the corrupt matter the flow of unlawful thought. Or the potsherd is mortal frailty, which he holds in his hand who always has it before his eyes, and by considering how soon it is to be dissolved he scrapes away the corrupt matter. Corrupt matter from a wound, a wicked thought from temptation: even if it is not brought to effect, yet it is not to be thought of as little. Whence: “whosoever shall look on a woman to lust after her,” etc. So fault must be cut away not only from the deed but also from the thought. Hence the angel appears to Jerobaal (Gedeon) threshing in the floor, who, rising, sacrifices a kid upon a rock. After the victim he poured out the broth of the flesh, the thoughts coming from fleshliness, which he also slays with the fleshliness. But because battle arises from victory, so that when a thought is overcome the mind is buffeted by pride, Job, scraping the matter, sits laid low in humility on a dunghill, that is, he thinks humbly of himself, and looks back with penance on what he has done amiss, lest any pride arise.
25_interl1928: see, scourges must be weighed by these two, their quantity [and their weight]; they are lightened if they are many and not heavy, or if heavy and not many
25_interl1930: he increases his abasement, to show himself humbler
25_marg654: Historically. A potsherd is made of clay, and the matter of the body is clay. So he wiped clay with clay, with a fragment of an earthen vessel, considering, in a broken earthen vessel, what he is who in carelessness swells. For through the things about the body the mind is puffed up, forgetful of human frailty, as happens in honours. Job, from the evils about him, increases his abasement, and sits not on clean ground but on a dunghill, weighing what the substance of the flesh is, and from the stench of the place he feels that the flesh will soon return to stench. What softness did he give his healthy flesh, who put to his wound not cloth or fingers but a potsherd? But the just man is pressed down here by God so that he may be gloriously rewarded; and it is shown what the wicked may expect, when he whom the judge praises is so pressed.
25_marg655: Allegorically. He took a potsherd. The potsherd in his hand is Christ’s flesh, from the clay of our substance, which, baked in the fire of the passion, rose stronger; with it he wiped away the corrupt matter, that is, sin. By flesh and blood also the sins of the flesh are marked; corrupt matter, from putrid blood, signifies sins made worse by age. Sitting on a dunghill, because “the weak things of the world hath God chosen”: having spurned the proud Jews, he rests among the gentiles, that is, among penitents, who by weeping over their evils heap up their dung before them, as it were, by casting themselves down. But he who did so much for men endures much in his members from the fleshly, who are like a wife in the bosom of the Church by faith; and so with evil ways and words they press harder, and, received as it were into the bed of faith, they cannot be escaped. These are the crowd that presses on Jesus, but only the humble woman touches him. These urge evils, either from fear, like Peter while still fleshly: “Lord, be it far from thee”; or from pride, like Joab the son of Sarvia asking David for the death of Semei. But worse are those who do it from pride, like Job’s wife, who in pride counsels her husband.
25_marg656: Allegorically. He shows that the devil’s first temptation was made in Job’s possessions and sons; the second he shows in the affliction of the body and the persuasion of his wife, and in a fitting order. For if he had first been afflicted in body he would have thought little afterwards of the taking away of his goods. The devil keeps back the wife, so as to conquer at least through her, he who conquered the first man through his wife; but as Job stood victor in the first temptation, so he remained victor in this. In the same way in Christ: first he is tempted in the apostles, he is afflicted in his own person, and in his members; and Christ is received whole.
25_marg657: And his wife said to him, etc. The devil attacks in two ways: by tribulation, to break, by persuasion, to soften. So, beaten in tribulation, he runs back to the art by which he conquered Adam, and to the height by a ladder, that is, through the woman, who, being near the man, tries to creep up on him. But he does not hear her as one set over him, but teaches her as one subject to him; and so he takes the weapons from the enemy, and they become weapons of virtue for him as he instructs her.
25_marg658: Morally. Even in prosperity, yet more amid the ills of the body, fleshly suggestion touches the mind. This is the wife who after the wounds counsels Job ill. Hence Jeremias: “Abroad the sword destroyeth” (that is, outward vengeance strikes), “and at home there is death alike,” because even then the conscience is not clean of temptations. But even if this suggestion wearies the good man and sometimes carries him off to delight, he soon blushes and rebukes himself, saying: “Thou hast spoken like one of the foolish women,” and fortifies himself by considering the gifts: “If we have received good things,” etc. But when someone, seeing so many vices besetting him, fortifies himself the more with virtues, certain vices come at him under the guise of virtues, that is, the friends meet as though to comfort, but break out into insults: as immoderate anger would seem justice, and loose remissness mercy, and fear humility, and unbridled pride freedom. Such begin with a smooth surface, but slide into harshness.
25_marg659: Allegorically. She reproves his simplicity, because he despises earthly things and desires eternal. As if to say: why do you simply seek eternal things and groan badly over these? Falling away (despise the eternal) escape present evils, or escape by dying. But those who suffered these things are a pattern of uprightness to them. Whence he says: “Like one of the foolish,” etc. Struck outwardly they endure the perverse; inwardly they teach: there strong, here merciful; there they drive back enemies, here they protect their own; and it is a great thing to do both in the battle line.
25_interl1931: by death you will end this affliction; or “die,” that is, you will live, by contraries
25_interl1932: that is, the gifts of God, that is, temporal or eternal
25_marg660: If we have received good things: that is, if we are making for eternal goods, why should we not bear present evils?
25_marg661: In all: because the saints, in all that they suffer outwardly and inwardly, do not go too far either at God’s wrongs or at the insults of the wicked.
25_marg662: “Dost thou still continue?” She repeats Eve’s words, as if saying: forsake simplicity, that is, despise obedience by eating what is forbidden. “Bless God and die,” that is, by overstepping the commandment live beyond what you were made.
25_marg663: See the order: after the wounds the enemy brought in words, because when the force of pain grows heavier, a wicked persuasion more easily takes hold of someone; for this reason he who took away the rest kept back the wife.
25_marg664: Because the fault is in the understanding, not the sex, he does not say ‘one of the women’ but ‘one of the foolish women’; for to think wickedly belongs to a folly that has befallen, not to the condition of nature.
25_marg665: If we have received good things: it is a great comfort in evils to remember goods, lest there be utter despair; as in times of joy the foresight of evil tempers pride. Whence it is said: “In the day of good things be not unmindful of evils: and in the day of evils be not unmindful of good things.”
25_marg666: We sin with our lips in two ways: when we say unjust things, or when we keep silent about just things. But Job neither said proud things against the one who struck him nor kept silent about right things against the one who counselled him. He had patience, giving thanks to God, and taught, by reproving his wife’s folly; and so the beaten enemy is roused the more fiercely, and because the wife has been silenced he stirs up others to insults.
25_interl1935: because he could not be overcome by the things above, he therefore attacked him with others, namely friends, so that they might afterwards be believed
25_marg667: Allegorically. The friends signify the heretics, who meet for contention against the body of Christ, that is, against the afflicted Church, grieving at the falls of her members and bearing with others under the name of Christ; which is an increase of grief. From their own place, which is pride, for unless they swelled in heart they would not strive to assert wicked things; conversely the place of the good is humility. So they come from their place, because they are moved by pride against the Church, and their perverse action is gathered from their names. Eliphaz, Baldad, Sophar, as was said above, and the places they come from fit. Theman: ‘southern’; Suhe: ‘speaking’; Naama: ‘comeliness’. He comes from the south who desires more ardently to be wise than he ought; and they desire this heat of wisdom not to live well but to speak proudly. Hence they take on comeliness, that is, the appearance of the good, from learning: hypocrites, not wishing to be learned, but to seem so.
25_marg668: Heard. Morally. He does not say they heard because these vices hear, but the devil, who tempts by them, understands these things.
25_marg669: This number, morally or mystically, signifies the three troops of the Chaldeans, that is, the attack that is made in deed, word and thought; for he attacks all these.
25_interl1940: the scattering of the watchtower, or scattering the watchman
25_interl1942: They had made an appointment both among themselves and toward the stricken man; this shows how great was their charity; but their good intention is darkened by an indiscretion that sprang up
25_marg670: They had made an appointment: because they agree in falsehood, and while they teach their own doctrine they seem to comfort. But they truly comfort in present affliction who instruct about eternal things. The heretics are called friends because they are to be named not from their wickedness but from our kindness, as: “Friend, whereto art thou come?”
25_marg671: They had made an appointment, because certain vices join with one another against us, such as pride and anger, remissness and fear, which, though they are different, yet tend to the same end, that is, the overthrow of the spiritual Job.
25_interl1943: Morally. The vices lift up their eyes when, under the guise of virtues, they prepare to ensnare the faithful and pretend, as it were, to counsel them
25_marg672: Allegorically. Those who are below lift up their eyes if they consider the deeds of the Church; and her, placed in grief, who spurns these things and seeks the eternal, they do not know, because what they see in her they do not read again in their own heart; they who love these things despise the eternal. The garments of the heretics are those who cling to them in concord, who always rush into worse things and are divided from one another into many parts. When the garments are rent the body is shown, because when their followers are cut off by discord the malice is laid bare which was covered by concord.
25_marg673: But if from the distress of vices and the love of zeal we grieve within, the things that creep in on the glad do not prevail with the sad; whence he adds: “And when they had lifted up,” etc. The vices do not know the afflicted, from whom, rejected, they spring back, though they knew, that is, penetrated, the glad; and the more the devil sees himself detected in them, the more he hides them under the image of virtues. And this is: “And crying out they wept”: piety is signified by the weeping, discretion by the rending of the garments, the zeal of works by the dust on the heads, humility by the sitting. The appearance of piety leads to cruelty, if it forbids a fault to be punished by discipline, so that afterwards it is punished eternally. Discretion deceives, as if for weakness we take more food, as though discreetly, and indiscreetly stir up the wars of the flesh. Sometimes zeal for good works makes for the restlessness of toil. Humility kills usefulness, when a man thinks himself weaker and more useless than he is and ceases to profit others. But compunction subtly examines these vices lurking under the guise of virtues; for he who truly grieves within foresees well what is to be done outwardly and what is not; and every din of suggestions falls silent by the force of compunction. Whence: “No man spoke; for they saw his grief.” For if the heart truly grieves, the vices do not clamour against us. But the vices themselves are often changed to the use of virtues: as anger, if subjected to reason, is turned to the service of holy zeal; pride, if it bows to the fear of God, defends justice with free authority; strength of body, wicked before, if it is converted, profits much in the exercise of good works. Hence Job sacrifices for his friends, and those whom he bore as enemies he receives as fellow citizens through sacrifice; for when we subdue evil thoughts and turn them into virtues, we change enemies into friends, as it were, through the victim of the intention.
25_interl1944: because they had not seen him further in this state
25_interl1945: they take Job’s show of misery upon themselves, so as to be better believed
25_marg674: Historically. Because the plague had changed the appearance of the stricken man, a voluntary grief changes the appearance of the comforters; for he cannot comfort a grieving man who does not join in his grief, but draws him by clinging to it. So seeing his body torn they rend their garments; seeing him changed they defile their heads with dust; so that Job may the more readily hear them when he sees something of his own affliction in them. Yet the comforter must see to it that by grieving too much he does not weigh down the afflicted and drive the grieving man to despair; perhaps Job’s friends grieved too much, not knowing the mind of the stricken man, as though he had fallen away in heart.
25_marg675: Dust: earthly understanding; the head: the mind; heaven: the commandment of the word from above. To throw dust upon the head towards heaven is to corrupt the mind with worldly understanding and to think earthly things about heavenly words. Day: understanding; night: ignorance; seven: the whole.
25_marg676: So they sit, that is, they pretend to stoop to the weakening Church, both in the things in which they understand the true light and in those in which they have ignorance; and so they prepare the snares of deceit. On the ground, because they show an appearance of humility, so as to urge proud things; or the ground is the incarnation of Christ, which some heretics do not deny, but they differ from us either about the Godhead or about the manner of the incarnation; so because they do not deny it, they sit with Job on the ground, as it were. Days and nights, because whether in what they understand truly or in what they understand foolishly, they do not contradict the incarnation. No man spoke, because enemies are silent if we neglect to beget sons of God by preaching; but if we speak right things, then they heap grave insults on us and break out against us in a cry of grief. They speak indeed the seeds of errors when they see the hearts of the faithful grow numb; but when they see them minding high things, seeking from the distress of the world, with grief, a return to heaven, they warily bridle their tongue. And this is: “they saw that his grief was very great”; because they are afraid to speak wicked things when the grief of the love of God pierces hearts, because then they would not profit, and would lose even those they held, who are well trained.
25_marg677: It is not known whether they stayed continuously, or persisted for so many days with frequent visits.
25_marg678: No man spoke: for there are many who are slow to begin speaking but set no measure to what they have begun, speaking without discretion; and though they came with a good intention, headlong speech spoiled the good of a devout mind. Hence each must weigh the good he does in the scale of discretion, which is to divide what is offered; otherwise what is thought virtue is guilt. It was great charity to have come in concord to an afflicted friend; long-suffering to have kept silent with him so long; humility to have sat on the ground; compassion to have sprinkled their heads with dust; but because they spoke incautiously, what was well begun became evil at the end, and unless they are cleansed by sacrifice they must be punished.
25_marg679: After this Job opened, etc. He makes us attentive, as to hidden things which were covered in closed vessels, but are uncovered when their mouth is opened, so that we may be refreshed by their inmost fragrance. Up to here, a threefold exposition; from here on, as each place requires. He cursed his day: see, this is not according to the surface of the history, because it is both evil and impossible. For the day on which he was born no longer existed, and it is idle to curse a thing that does not exist, and harmful if it did exist; nor can a past day now be turned into darkness, nor can the rest that follows fit it; nor would an untimely birth (as he says afterwards) enjoy rest. So here nothing is according to the letter.
25_marg680: After this, that is, after all the things told above which he suffered, while even his friends were silent. So since he patiently gave thanks in all things and taught well, he is not now to be believed, with no one urging him, to break out into cursing from impatience; but he says this calmly, because amid evils he praised God.
25_marg681: A curse is spoken in two ways: by the judgment of justice, or by the spite of revenge. The first is praised, the second forbidden. God uses the first, as: “cursed is the earth in thy work,” “I will curse them that curse thee.” The saints too, seeing God’s judgment within, curse not with a wish for vengeance but with God’s justice. Whence Peter: “Keep thy money to thyself, to perish with thee.” And Elias to the two captains of fifty: “If I be a man of God, let fire come down … and consume thee.” Against the other kind, which is done in malice, the Apostle says: “bless, and curse not,” and: “nor railers … shall possess the kingdom of God.”
25_marg682: So Job’s curse is not malice but justice, not agitation but teaching. For he sees his friends weeping and, judging by themselves (they sought the prosperity of the world), thinking him broken by evils, and, knowing nothing of inner salvation, despairing and weeping for him on that account. And he lays down a remedy: “Let the day perish wherein I was born,” not made; for man was made on the day of justice, but born on the day of fault: Adam was made, Cain was the first born. So the day on which he was born is the whole time of mortality, under which eternity does not appear to those who live; let this, then, perish, and eternity appear. To perish is said in two ways: not to be, or to be in an evil state. This time of ours will so perish as not to be; whence “time shall be no longer.” For when it is said: “and their time shall be for ever,” it is put for failing, as time fails by moments; yet here he wishes it so to perish as to be in an evil state, for otherwise it could not be wrapped in bitterness, as he says afterwards. But the soul or an angel is so immortal that it cannot die. For it dies by vice or by punishment, by which it loses living in bliss; yet it never ceases to live in its essence. So the day he wishes to perish is the apostate angel, who has indeed already perished from glory, but it is still wished that, thrust back into punishments, he may lose even the leave to tempt. That day was well made by nature, a night by its deserts. The day is dark when it entices with prosperity, but ends in night because it draws to evils. It shows a day when it promises better things: “you shall be as Gods,” but brought on the night of mortality. A day when, promising good things, it appears as an angel of light; a night when it darkens the hearts of those who consent with errors. So Job, in his own grief weeping for the cause of the whole human race, brings back to mind the origin of fault, and tempers the grief of punishment by the consideration of justice. He sees whence man fell, and says: “Let the day perish, and the night in which,” etc., as if: let the hope brought by the devil perish, which shone with the promise of godhead, but like the night darkened immortality. Let the enemy perish who promised light but brought on the darkness of sin.
25_marg683: Job, seeing how much man, after his fall, is lifted up by prosperity and how much he is pressed by adversity, runs back to unchangeableness, and declares by cursing how much he despises this state. “Let the day perish”: the day is the prosperity of the world, which ends in night, because it leads to tribulation. Or the day is the delight of sin, the night the blindness of the mind. Man is spoken of in three ways: by nature, by fault, by weakness. So man is born in the day and conceived in the night, because he is not carried off to the delight of sin unless he is first weakened by the darkness of the mind. But let the day perish, that is, let the delight of sin be destroyed by the vigour of justice; and the night, that is, what the blinded mind commits by consent when it does not warily see through the allurements of delight, let penance extinguish. But lest the fault which begins to allure run on to destruction, “let the day be turned into darkness,” that is, at the beginning of the love let it be seen to what end of perdition it carries one away, and let it be tormented by penance. If it is so punished, “let not God regard it” in judgment to punish it, and “let not the light shine upon it.” He shines light upon one whom he reproves; but one is covered, as it were, who is not called back to the judge’s memory. Whence “whose sins are covered,” lest they be shown then in the sight of all. Let it not be shone upon, but let them cover it, that is, the day of delight, lest it be seen by him who sees all things. “Darkness,” that is, the laments of penance, or God’s hidden judgments, by which we are absolved, forestalled by grace, though we know not that we merit it; “and the shadow of death,” that is, the death of Christ according to the flesh, which destroyed our fault. Hence he was one day and two nights in the tomb, because he joined the light of his single death to the darkness of our fault. True death is called that by which the soul is separated from God; its shadow, that by which the flesh is separated from the soul. Otherwise the shadow of death is called forgetfulness, which makes a thing not to be in memory, as death makes what it takes not to be in life. Or the devil is called death, and his change, which is from his own form, as a shadow from a body, the shadow of death. But because no sin is unpunished, even where mercy helps, let man punish this; whence follows: “let a mist overspread it,” that is, confusion of mind, of which it is said: “there is a shame that bringeth glory”; “and let it be wrapped up” on every side in the bitterness of penance. But if the day, that is, the delight of sin, is so punished, what of the night, that is, consent to the fault?
25_interl1947: first of the day, afterwards of the night
25_interl1948: let it be so understood, namely that the prosperity it promises be understood as adversity; for as the enemy is when raging, so is he when flattering
25_interl1949: that is, let the blindness of its error so overwhelm it that it may not rise again to the light of penance through God’s remembrance
25_interl1950: that is, forgetfulness, which blots out memory as death blots out life
25_interl1951: now because it has fallen from the light, now it is confounded within by mist
25_interl1952: afterwards it will be tormented with the endless punishment of hell; for what is wrapped up does not show its end; and this punishment will begin when the judge comes
25_interl1953: let the tempest carry off the apostate angel from the sight of the judge to punishments; of which it is said: “and a mighty tempest shall be round about him”
25_marg684: Like the whirlwind of a storm is the roused spirit of mourning, which clouds the mind with sadness. This is the spirit that breaks the ships of Tharsis, that is, the force of compunction, which confounds with wholesome terror minds given to the sea, that is, to the world.
25_marg685: Let not … regard it: man is redeemed because, being flesh and spirit, he had something weak by which he sinned, which an angel had not; besides, the angel perished by his own malice, man by another’s. So he says “let not God regard it”; and because it brought on darkness, let it bear without end what it did, nor receive the light which it lost without being persuaded.
25_marg686: Morally. He who flatters himself in sin is possessed by the night; he who punishes it possesses the night, and better if the sin is held down as it begins. But what we punish, we hope will not be thrown up to us by the judge; whence “let it not be counted,” etc. The year of our enlightenment is completed when the judge comes and the pilgrimage is finished. The days of the year are the several virtues; the months are the manifold deeds of the virtues, or the collection of the virtues of each good man. But because with these he fears lest the judge weigh the evils too, he prays that then he may so reward the good as not to look into the evil. For if this night is numbered with the days, all things are now darkened; and that it may not be numbered then, let us examine it now, lest any fault be unpunished, lest anyone defend what he has done, adding wickedness to wickedness. Whence he adds: “Let that night be solitary, and not worthy of praise.” For there are those who praise and defend evil things, and so the fault is doubled and does not remain solitary. Against which it is said: “Hast thou sinned? do so no more.” To sin, that is, to defend evil, as Adam did, who, sought out for penance, added an excuse to his fault: “The woman, whom thou gavest me,” etc., as if: you were the occasion of sin, who gave the woman. But he pursues fault well who desires no prosperity of the world. Whence it is said: “Let them curse it who curse the day”; that is: they strike the night well by penance who trample on the light of prosperity, who do not have the day of delight. Or the day is the enemy’s suggestion; and they truly punish it as done who in his very smooth suggestion detect the snares of the deceiver, who rouse Leviathan the more against themselves. For others, whom he possesses securely, he sleeps; but for these he wakes for every battle. But because when the vices are conquered some very small thing remains which cannot be conquered, lest the victor be lifted up, he adds: “Let the stars be darkened with the mist of that night”; because even if they shine with virtues they drag remnants of the night, even resisting, so that from it they may shine better; whence, unwilling, they are humbly darkened. Hence the Chanaanite, not slain, becomes tributary to the tribe of Ephraim in the land of promise; because when we enter heavenly things with hope, vices remain among the best things, which yet serve us for the use of humility, lest he be proud who cannot conquer even small things. Whence again: “These are the nations which the Lord left, that by them he might instruct Israel,” that is, vices in which virtue is always exercised; and while it fears to be conquered the pride of virtue is held down, and in small things it learns that it does not by itself conquer greater. Or “let the stars be darkened with the mist of that night,” because the night, that is, consent to fault, handed down from Adam to us, so troubles the eye that even those who shine in the world like stars cannot see the eternal light as it is. And this is: “let it expect light and not see it”; because with however much ardour they leap up, yet in this flesh they will not see the light as it is, because of the blindness of condemnation in which we are born.
25_marg687: Allegorically. The year is grace from above, in which is the manifold life of the virtues, like days in the year. Or the year is the multitude of the redeemed, which is completed by the gathering of all the good, as the year by its days; which in Isaias is called “the acceptable year of the Lord.” The days are the several elect; the months, the many churches which make one catholic Church. But the night is not counted among these, that is, the devil; because he beholds the coming of Christ, but does not believe in it unto pardon with the elect. Whence “nowhere doth he take hold of the angels.” Or the days are the angelic spirits remaining in the light; the months their orders and dignities, such as the thrones and the rest; but the devil is brought back neither to the light nor to their order, but is shut out from that homeland for ever. Whence he adds: “Let that night be solitary,” because it is separated from that throng; or he loses man, whom he had made his companion, and, when the elect are redeemed by grace, he is handed over alone with his body to hell.
25_marg688: Not worthy of praise: man, when laid low, worshipped idols, in which he praised the demons as the darkness of the night; but now that the idols are rejected it is not worthy of praise.
25_marg689: Let them curse it who, etc. In the old translation: “Let him curse it who curseth the day, who is ready to take the great whale.” The devil, who now lies hidden as night, at the end will be seen as day, when he will be lifted up above all that is called God or worshipped. But now he destroys his malice who at the end will destroy his power by his coming; who in the waters (namely of baptism) extinguishes the great whale, that is, his strength. Or “let them curse it,” that is, the night, the elect angels, announcing its darkness by condemning it, “who curse the day,” that is, who show that its feigned brightness, by which it presumed to become equal to God, is to be despised; “who are ready to raise up,” that is, to let loose, so that he may act with all his strength against the Church; for now he is held bound in the abyss and pressed down; and he who proudly lifted himself above the others has sunk, laid low, under their rule, so that now, bound by their ministry, he lies hidden, and at the end, loosed, he will wage open war.
25_marg690: Leviathan: that is, ‘their addition’, that is, of men, in whom after suggestion he does not cease to add evils. Or ‘reproach’, because when he promised to add godhead to Adam he also took away what he had. He is called by the prophet the crooked serpent, because he is soft, pouring in snares as through the smooth coils of words; and a bar, because he is hard through malice and strikes to death. When roused he will act openly; meanwhile, secretly. “With the mist of that night let the stars be darkened,” that is, the hypocrites, who shine by their works to the eyes of men. These are they whom the tail of the dragon, that is, the final persecution of Antichrist, draws; these are darkened, because the enemy’s malice so prevails over them that they are wrapped in open evils, being outwardly what they are within.
25_marg691: Let it expect light: this is according to his members, that is, the wicked who have faith and either do wicked things or good things with no right heart; and secure, because in their own and many people’s opinion they are holy, they await the day of the Lord, not in vain indeed. Of them the prophet says: “Woe to them that desire the day of the Lord.” The light, then, that is, Christ, who says: “I am the light of the world.” The dawn rising is the Church, which forsakes the former darkness and comes into the light of justice. Its rising is the beginning of eternal brightness. So in the judgment there is still dawn, in the kingdom day, whose rising in the light of the Lord’s coming the wicked will not see, because, pressed by darkness, they will not know with how great a light it rises. Whence: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God.” Or in the present they do not see the rising of the dawn who, when they see works, do not weigh the intention, imitating what they may be praised for outwardly, not what may raise them within to the light. Or this is a prophecy of Judea, which awaited Christ by prophesying, but did not know him when he came.
25_marg692: Nor the rising of the dawning of the day. Morally. The rising of the dawn is the new birth of the resurrection, by which the saints will rise with the flesh to see the eternal light. But however much the elect shine here, they cannot penetrate what that glory of the new birth will be to them. This night did not shut but opened the doors of the womb, because it unlocked the desires of concupiscence to human conception unto sin. And when these doors, that is, the desires of fleshly concupiscence, are unlocked, we are dragged to countless evils of corruption. Whence, weighed down, we groan; because justice requires that what we did willingly we should bear unwillingly.
25_marg693: Because it shut not up: this is of the head itself. Paradise is the womb from which the human race came forth, growing by its offspring, conceived there in Adam its origin. The serpent opened its doors, because he burst into the bars of the mind, fortified by warnings from above, and dissolved God’s commandment in it. So Job, in his punishment, thinks again on the fault, and grieves at what the night, that is, the enemy’s dark suggestion, brought into the minds of men, and that man consented to him. He says that he did not shut who opened, and did not take away who brought on; because he would, as it were, take away if he kept still, and would shut if he ceased from bursting in; for the wicked one would, as it were, have been giving us gain if he had not brought losses, as we say robbers give life to their captives if they do not take it away.
25_marg694: Why did I not die in the womb? It is not to be believed that so great a man wishes he had perished as an untimely birth; but these words are to be weighed inwardly. Sin is done in the heart in four ways, and completed in deed in four. In the heart there is suggestion, by the enemy, as the serpent persuaded in paradise; then delight, through the flesh, as there too Eve was delighted; afterwards consent, by the spirit, as there too Adam consented; then defence, through pride, as Adam too, when sought out, excused himself; he feared indeed, but also swelled. For when punishment is feared but the face of God, being lost, is not loved, fear is from swelling, not from humility; because he is proud who does not forsake sin if he may go unpunished. In deed, first the fault is committed in secret; afterwards it is laid open before men without shame; then it is brought into habit; afterwards it is fed either by false hope or by despair. In so many ways the human race weeps for its fall. “Why did I not die in the womb?” The womb in which man is conceived in sin is evil suggestion; but would that he had died in it, that is, had known that he would die, lest the suggestion draw him to delight.
25_marg695: When I came out of the belly. Morally. Because delight snatched the conceived sin outside; but [why did I not] fall in that delight rather than lose my wits as far as consent to the deed? He was received on the knees, because through the consent of the spirit, with all the senses subject to it as knees, he completed the fault. He was also suckled at the breasts, when he is fostered by empty confidence and smooth excuses. So too in deed. The womb is hidden fault. He comes out who does not blush to do openly what he did in secret; whence: “they have proclaimed abroad their sin as Sodom.” But why did I not wish to put myself to death from the life of the flesh in hidden iniquity, or, when I came out into action, why did I not at least then know myself lost? He is fostered on the knees to grow who, not ashamed of his open evil, is strengthened by wicked habits, so as to thrive for worse things. But why these things? that is, would it were not so! He is suckled, because after the fault has come into habit he feeds himself with false hope of God’s mercy, lest he return to amendment; for after habit, even if he wishes, a man resists sin more weakly; whence, enervated, he bends to false comforts, as though God spares these things too; to which is added the flattery of many like him; whence: “if sinners shall entice thee, consent not to them.” Besides, despair feeds the soul with the milk of error. The first three ways, in their order, are more easily corrected, the fourth with more difficulty. Hence Christ raised three dead: in the house, one who lies hidden in sin; outside the gate, one whose iniquity is made public; buried under the mound, that is, one weighed down by the mass of habit. A fourth he hears of as dead and does not raise, because one pressed by evil habit hardly rises again if he is fed with flattery; which is: “let the dead bury their dead,” that is, overwhelm them with favours; or if despair feeds the soul with the milk of error. So Job sees to what great precipices of this exile man has come down, after he lost paradise through fault, and accuses himself of having sinned in the first parent. If that had not been, he adds what rest he could have enjoyed: “For now I should have been asleep and still, and should have rest in my sleep”: if man had not sinned in paradise, he would at some time have passed without death to the homeland of the angels, to which the redeemed are to be carried after death; and had fault not come forth, the saints would rest in peace of heart, and, all clamour, unrest and tumult of temptations removed, would withdraw within the secret of the mind to the contemplation of God; who now cry out as though awake, while they bear the strife of their own flesh against the spirit.
25_marg696: By “now,” which belongs to the present time, he signifies what stands always in the present, that is, eternal rest.
25_interl1959: I would rest in eternal goods
25_interl1960: by despising the tumult of earthly desires
25_marg697: Should have rest with kings: that is, with the angels, who rule those beneath them; who are also consuls, because they counsel us by announcing God’s will. Or he calls kings the holy preachers, who rule themselves; and consuls of the earth, because they counsel earthly men well. So he says that if man had not sinned, he would have gone up, even unredeemed, to where the apostles and holy preachers arrive after the redemption with great labour; who are not kept waiting like the ancients, but enter heaven soon after death. “Who build themselves solitudes”: every earthly man is crushed in heart by dense tumults of thoughts, and trampled by the press of desires as by crowds. But to build solitudes is to drive the tumults of earthly desires from the secret of the heart and to pant for the love of inward rest, so that one can say: “One thing I have asked … this will I seek after,” etc.
25_marg698: With princes, that possess gold. The princes are the rulers of the Church. Gold: wisdom, by which eternal goods are bought, as temporal ones with gold. The houses are the consciences. Silver: the divine words. So the princes, that is, the rulers succeeding in the place of the apostles, possess gold by living wisely, and fill the house of conscience with the divine words with which they instruct them. So Job, foreseeing the future, considers with wonder with which elect he would have rested in eternity without toil, had no one sinned through pride. And he says: “For now I should have been asleep and still,” etc.; because if no rottenness of sin had corrupted Adam, he would not have begotten from himself sons of hell, but those alone would have been born from him as elect who are now to be saved by redemption. He who foresaw the future now recalls the past.
25_marg699: Or as an untimely birth: because what is born untimely, before its time, is dead and at once hidden away. These are the saints with whom he considered he could have rested, who were from the beginning of the world before the time of the redemption, and yet put themselves to death to the world. The first time, before the law, which brought forth fathers dead to the world, was as the womb of an untimely birth; and they themselves were as dead from the womb, who without the tables of the law feared God by nature and, believing in the Redeemer to come, slew their pleasures.
25_marg700: Hidden: because, few being recorded by Moses, the greater part of them is withdrawn from knowledge; and they are said no longer to exist, because their great number is kept in no written record among us. Or those who, conceived through the law, did not see the light of the Lord’s coming, to which, faithfully believed in, they could not attain. In them the inward conception produced the form of faith, but did not bring it to fitting sight. Now he lays open the rest of this light, and shows in plainer words what is daily done there concerning the conduct of the wicked.
25_marg701: Or as they that being conceived: we call ‘conceived’ not only those who had the written law, but all from Abraham, to whom the promises were openly made, whom the spirit of prophecy shone upon, as Job himself.
25_interl1967: in respect of this light and rest
25_interl1968: in a manner, in the present
25_interl1969: in the hope of that light
25_marg702: There the wicked cease from tumult: that is, in the light of Christ, for which the ancients waited, the gentiles cease from the crowd of the world’s desires, and with a calm mind already foretaste eternal rest. And this is: “and there the wearied in strength are at rest.” Those strong in the unclean world are said to be not wearied in strength. He who is strengthened in the love of God wholesomely fails in his own strength, and the more strongly he seeks the eternal, the more, wearied, he dies to earthly things. Whence: “My soul longeth and fainteth for the courts of the Lord.” By saying “there” he shows the light as the place in which the elect are held.
25_interl1972: in the rest of the saints
25_marg703: And they sometime bound: the just, though at rest from desires, are yet bound while in the body by the trouble of their corruption; for the body weighs down the soul and the flesh fights against the spirit. There are bodily bonds too: hunger, thirst and the like, which cannot be loosed here, but they will be loosed from all of them “into the liberty of the glory of the children of God.” See the steps: the wicked, converted, cease; the trained rest in the inmost bosom; loosed from the bonds of corruption, they come to freedom. But what they do here meanwhile he adds: “they have not heard the voice of the oppressor.” The oppressor is the devil, who once paid man the coin of deception and daily exacts the debt of death. His voice is temptation: he hears who is tempted and resists; he hearkens who consents. The same is said of inward peace, because what the mind greatly loves it repeats more often.

It is a small animal which, hiding in the dust, lies in wait for ants and eats them; but to birds and other animals it is an ant, by which it is eaten. By this he notes that Job was timid against the lofty and bold against those under him; but now his pride has no prey, because, being struck, he is kept from hurting others.

25_marg729: There was a word spoken to me: the Son of God; “in private,” because he “was with God.” This is said to the faithful when he is made known to believers. Or the word is the speech of inward inspiration through the Spirit hidden in the heart, which cannot be known except by him who can have it. Whence of this Spirit it is said: “whom the world cannot receive,” because it loves visible things, while the Spirit ascends to invisible things alone. So what few hear within is unknown to the greatest part of men. Or “in private,” because it sounds silently in the heart without the din of speech. “And by stealth as it were,” because swiftly and secretly; for unless the mind is hidden from outward things it does not penetrate inward ones. It receives not the whisper but its veins. The whisper is the inward speech itself; the veins are the ways by which it comes to our mind, because sometimes it pricks us with love, sometimes with terror, and in other ways. So to hear the veins of the whisper by stealth is to know faintly and secretly the hidden ways of divine inspiration. Or he who whispers speaks secretly and does not utter his voice but imitates it. So when God now intimates something of himself to us, he whispers, not as he is; but he will speak in the future, when he shows himself as he is. Or the veins of the whisper are all created things, by which we gather knowledge of the Godhead. But these too by stealth, because we weigh even his wonderful works only swiftly and faintly; but the more the uplifted mind considers God’s power, the more, held back, it dreads his uprightness. Whence he adds: “In the horror of a vision by night,” etc., that is, in the dread of hidden contemplation, in which nothing is seen plainly, but as it were in images. But to this none attains unless fleshly desires are held down. Whence: “when deep sleep is wont to hold men.” He is awake who attends to the cares of the world; he sleeps who flees them restlessly. This is Jacob, who sleeps on his journey and sees angels; that is, in the course of this life he closes his eyes to worldly things, which fault opened in the first parents to covet. And no one is brought to see inward things unless he is withdrawn from the things that entangle outwardly; whence: “Be still and see that I am God.” But the more the mind, raised in contemplation, beholds higher things above itself, the more terribly it trembles in itself. Whence: “Fear seized upon me … and all my bones,” that is, the stronger deeds; because they do not think their good things worthy of the examination of him whom they behold, which by themselves seemed of some value. Whence it is said: “All my bones shall say: Lord, who is like to thee?” The flesh has no word, because weak things are wholly silent before you; but the strong things praise the great one and tremble. Hence it is that Manue, having seen the angel, fears, but the woman dares; because when heavenly things are seen, the spirit which sees first is struck with dread, but yet hope presumes; because hope rises up to greater things from that by which the spirit is troubled. So because, when God’s justice is seen, our goods too seem foul, he rightly says: “Fear seized upon me, and all my bones were affrighted.” Hence Paul too, not conscious to himself of his merits, does not presume with God as judge. But when the uplifted mind gazes on inward things it cannot stand above itself for long, because, if the spirit carries it to the heights, the flesh weighs it down by the weight of its corruption. Whence: “And when a spirit passed before me.” The spirit passes while we are present, because we see invisible things not steadily but swiftly; nor is the mind fixed long in the sweetness of contemplation, because, beaten back by the light, it is called back to itself; and, advancing with great strength, it sees that it cannot see what it ardently loves; yet it would not love ardently unless it saw to some extent. And because however much one has advanced he feels the goad of the flesh, he adds: “the hair of my flesh stood up.” The hairs are any superfluities of human corruption, the thoughts of the old life; if we shut these out of the mind we cut the hairs from the flesh, so that we are not wearied by pain. Whence Moses: “let the Levites shave all the hairs of their flesh.” But we see these more subtly in ourselves when we penetrate high things; whence it is rightly said now: “when a spirit passed, the hair of my flesh stood up.” For when the mind sees true things it torments itself more harshly over superfluous ones. So when the spirit passes the hairs are terrified, because before the force of compunction superfluous thoughts flee; because the inward vision kindles the soul against itself, and when it strictly cuts away unlawful things, the mind clings more broadly to contemplation, and almost fixes the spirit that was passing; yet even this lingering of contemplation does not fully lay open the power of the Godhead. Whence he adds: “There stood one whose countenance I knew not.” ‘One’ is said only of him whom we either will not or cannot express; and so here he explains: “whose countenance I knew not”; because man, who by obeying was to become spiritual even in the flesh, by sinning was made fleshly even in mind, so that he thinks only what he draws into the mind through images of the body; but hardly, by striving, with bodily form held down, does he know himself; and so a way is made for him to think of the eternal substance, and, all imaginings cast off, he beholds it to some extent; and even if he does not grasp what it is, he certainly knows what it is not. He seems to stand, since all things pass except those he keeps in himself, as the good. Hence when he says “when a spirit passed” he rightly adds “there stood one,” as if: him whom I felt in passing I found does not pass. He passes, because he cannot be held when known; he stands, because he is known to be unchangeable. But because whoever grasps anything of him beholds it through his coeternal image, he adds: “an image before my eyes.” The image of the Father is the Son, who says: “No man cometh to the Father, but by me.” “And I heard the voice as it were of a gentle wind.” The voice of the wind is the knowledge of the Holy Spirit, who is said to be both gentle and vehement upon the apostles; because he tempers his knowledge to us so that he can be known in some fashion, and not as he is, but slips faintly in, as to the bleary-eyed; vehement, because he who touches gently shakes our poverty mightily. So because the mind of man, however much it stretches itself, hardly ever sees anything of him, it is rightly said: “and the voice as it were of a wind”; but because even a little of divine knowledge teaches us perfectly, he adds what he learned from this hearing:
