25_interl2047: it troubles the wise but does not kill him
25_marg739: Anger, etc. After the mockery he adds a sentence which is true, but wrongly applied to Job: “Anger killeth the foolish.” Meekness keeps in us the image of God, who is always calm; but anger scatters it, depriving us of many virtues, because while it takes quiet from the mind, the Holy Spirit does not rest there. But one anger is that which impatience makes, another that which zeal makes. The first comes from vice, the second from virtue, which Phinees had; with this we ought to be angry at the errors of our neighbours as at our own; it is “better than laughter, because by the sadness of the countenance” the neighbour “is corrected.” But it must not rule the mind, but be subject to reason as a handmaid; let it not be immoderate, but in avenging sin consider time and measure, first conquering itself by patience. This anger troubles the wise; but anger through vice slaughters the foolish.
25_interl2048: the lower; or the one who loves eternal things
25_marg740: And envy slayeth the little one: that is, while he envies one he thinks greater, as the devil envied man, Cain his brother, whose sacrifice he grieved to see preferred, and Esau too his brother. So the little one is slain by envy, because unless he were lower he would not grieve at another’s good. Or the little one is he who loves earthly things, the great one he who loves eternal things. So the little one is slain by envy, because no one dies of this plague except him who craves these earthly things, which do not come whole to many. Hence, if we desire anything, we envy him who receives it wholly, or who, by having a part, narrows the amount for us.
25_marg741: I have seen a fool with a strong root. Morally. Because he is made solid with all his desires in earthly love. Hence Cain first built a city on earth. The stranger to heaven lives more happily here.
25_marg742: And I cursed: because when, at the sight of the prosperity of the wicked, the feet of the weak stagger, the strong, seeing what punishment follows on their glory, at once reject their prosperity. The weak man changes with the state of things: while he sees prosperity he praises it; when it changes he judges it to be nothing. But the firm man considers, along with the glory itself, the punishment that follows, and at once condemns it. But because those who prosper in the world draw many with them, he adds: “His children shall be far,” that is, his followers.
25_marg743: The gate of the kingdom is the day of judgment, in which the elect enter into glory; before it the children of this world are fools, but then they will be destroyed.
25_interl2056: of old, judges sat in the gates of cities, taking care that no one should enter unjustly or be driven out from there
25_marg744: And there shall be none to deliver them: because there the truth delivers those whom here it presses down by discipline.
25_marg745: Whose harvest: each one has a house of understanding, by which he understands and speaks right things. But because he neither loves nor does them, he fasts from the harvest he has; but he who hungers for justice, hearing right things from him, refreshes himself; whence: “What they say, do.”
25_interl2062: with the weapons of pestilent persuasion
25_interl2063: the devil is armed when he bends the wise to himself, deceiving not openly but secretly
25_marg746: And the armed man shall take him by violence: the devil is beaten as one unarmed when, suggesting open evils, he tries to take away all good things at once. But he comes armed when he passes by some good things untouched and secretly corrupts others.
25_marg747: And the thirsty shall drink up: the fool often has riches, a gift of understanding and the sacred words, but does not drink, because he does not exercise himself in them. But another, who has no such gift, has thirst, and by loving and studying attains what the gifted man does not know. This is “the stellio,” as Solomon says, which “supporteth itself on hands, and dwelleth in kings’ houses.” For he helps his understanding with his hands, and leaning on his hands holds the building of the kingdom, like the stellio, a creature that has no wings for flight. But sometimes birds that have wings, that is, the gifted, sit in the brambles. But because it would be asked why the gift is given to the negligent and the studious man is held back by slowness, he answers:
25_interl2064: the slothful man receives the gift so that he may be punished more justly for his negligence
25_marg748: Nothing upon earth is done without a cause: because thereby the one is more justly punished for negligence, the other crowned for his study. But because we are taught to understand right things not only by study but also by persecutions, he adds:
25_marg749: And sorrow doth not spring out of the ground: the ground, that is, the elements of the world, are turned into the punishment of offenders. Whence it is said: “the whole world shall fight with him,” that is, for the Lord, “against the unwise.” But sorrow will not spring only from them, because punishment is not born of the things that strike, but of those who by sinning forced out the blows. But the more the outward punishment chastises, the more the mind is raised to things above; whence he adds:
25_interl2066: because the body is scourged so that the mind may fly to God
25_marg750: Man is born to labour and the bird to fly: because it is impossible to be without labour on this pilgrimage; but in that the flesh is afflicted, the mind is raised to seek high things. Or man, that is, the fleshly man, feels the evils of the world because he greedily craves its goods. But he whose mind passes beyond these, raised like a bird to the heights on the wing of hope, feels no evil, since he rejoices even in scourges. But because no one is able for these things by his own strength, he adds:
25_interl2069: that you too may fly to the labour
25_interl2070: by whom I know this is granted
25_marg751: That is, I ask him by whom I know these things are granted.
25_marg752: Who doth great things and unsearchable: which no one is able to search out, which are wonderful even if they have grown cheap by use. It would be of less greatness to do great things if anyone could search them out, and again of less greatness to do unsearchable things if they were few; and so he adds:
25_interl2072: these things can be understood of the elect, where the humble with lofty mind pass beyond all temporal things, and the afflicted are set upright by health, not by madness
25_marg753: Wonderful things without number: because the greatness of the divine works can neither be discussed as to their quality nor numbered as to their quantity.
25_marg754: I have seen a fool. Mystically. The fool is the people of the Jews, who scorned the wisdom of God in the flesh. “With a strong root,” because it overcame the elect by killing them; but the heretics too reprove its unbelief. This is what Eliphaz despises by cursing. The children are those it begets in unbelief. “Far from safety,” because even if happy here, they will afterwards be punished more heavily. “In the gate,” that is, in Christ, in whose presence the Jews fell who had flourished in the Law before his coming; whom no one delivers, because by killing the Redeemer they lost the deliverance offered them. “Whose harvest”: the harvest is the words of God, which, because the fool had them but did not eat, the hungry Gentile eats by understanding them; the harvest lost, he himself also perishes. “The armed man,” that is, the devil, carries him off by killing the life of faith in him. “The thirsty”: the Gentiles are watered by the streams of the sacred word. The same words are both harvest, because they refresh the fasting mind, and riches, because they order behaviour with great beauty.
25_marg755: Nothing upon earth is done without a cause: he puts this because some thought that all scourges come by natural causes, according to the nature of the elements, and not from the fault of the one struck.
25_marg756: Who giveth rain. Allegorically. These words are mystical, because Job’s friends had been taught by his company. He gives rain to the earth when he pours the grace of preaching into the dry hearts of the Gentiles.
25_marg757: Watereth all things with waters, when he fills man with the Spirit to bear fruit. Man is called all things because he has something in common with all things. Or all things, that is, rich and poor and all the differences of men, because reward follows a good work. He adds:
25_interl2074: those who despise temporal things he raises to heavenly ones
25_marg758: Who setteth up the humble on high, so that those now despised may judge with the Lord.
25_marg759: Those that mourn: because the more they are troubled now by adversity, and chastise themselves by lamenting, the loftier the health they will have, even in this life. These things can be understood of the elect, where the humble with lofty mind pass beyond all temporal things, and the afflicted are set upright by health, not by madness, like those who rejoice when they have done evil. But these grow cheerful from the certainty of eternal salvation.
25_marg760: Who bringeth to nought the designs of the malignant: when the reprobate devise evil, God sometimes, lest they prevail against the good, takes away their strength so that they lack the effect of the deed, and are guilty before God in conscience.
25_marg761: Who catcheth the wise in their craftiness, and disappointeth the counsel of the wicked: because human deeds serve God’s counsels fittingly even when they resist them; as in the selling of Joseph, so that he should not be worshipped; in Saul’s demand for foreskins, so that David should be destroyed; in the death of the Lord, so that not all should believe in him. God grants some things in mercy, permits others in anger, which he then turns to the use of his own counsel; so that the things which fight against his counsel serve his counsel, and what is done without his will is not contrary to his will. Whence: “Whatsoever the Lord pleased he hath done.”
25_marg762: They shall meet with darkness in the day. Mystically. Because in the very presence of the truth they were blinded by the error of unbelief, seeing the miracles of Christ and doubting his Godhead.
25_marg763: As in the night: by groping we seek what “we do not see with our eyes.” The Jews had seen miracles and still, as though groping, asked: “If thou be the Christ, tell us plainly.” But Christ could not be held long in their hands. Whence he adds:
25_marg764: But he shall save … from the sword of their mouth: the sword of the mouth is the accusation of the Jews. The hand of the violent: the Gentiles who crucified him. But Christ overcame these by rising again, in whom, the needy, that is, the humble people of the faithful, the hope of the life to come is made solid. But the iniquity which now opens its mouth wide in insult to Christ will shut it through punishment; or, converted, it ceases from its injuries.
25_marg765: The same things of the wicked in general. “They shall meet with darkness in the day.” The mind of the envious man, when it is pained at another’s good, is darkened by the ray of the sun. “And grope at noonday as in the night.” The day of good work shines outwardly in the neighbour, but they grope as in the night, because, blind with spite, they busy themselves to find something to blame. Behold Lot, that is, the just man, with the wicked opposing him, is shut within the house and protected, that is, he returns to his mind and stays within. The blind Sodomites go round about, that is, the envious search out his deeds and words, and do not find the door, that is, an opening for blame, but grope at the wall, because everywhere the praiseworthy action of the just man meets them. “They shall grope.” But the poor in spirit, that is, he who is not lifted up in himself, is saved “from the sword of their mouth,” that is, from wicked persuasion. “And the poor from the hand of the violent,” that is, from hostile power, so that he is neither drawn away by the flatteries of persuasion nor broken by the pain of torments. The poor man is not drawn away, because his hope, fixed in eternal things, is made solid against these. When the poor man comes to the fruit of this hope, the proud man falls dumb and draws in his mouth, because torments bind the tongue that spoke against the just in detraction. But that the elect may escape punishment and reach the reward, he must be purged here by scourges. Whence he adds: “Blessed is the man whom God correcteth.”
25_interl2084: God sometimes lets the soul be wounded by the longing of its desire, so that it may rise stronger and be healed
25_marg766: And because he is blessed: “refuse not therefore the chastising of the Lord.” He refuses it who complains that he suffers unjustly. So Eliphaz, thinking that Job is struck for cleansing, not for the proving of his fortitude, because Job speaks freely, asking the causes of his striking, thinks he refuses the chastising of the Lord. So heretics turn to evil what is rightly done by the Church.
25_marg767: For he woundeth: in two ways God wounds those whom he brings back to salvation. Sometimes he strikes in the body to heal the mind; sometimes, without outward scourges, he strikes the hardness of the mind with longing for himself, and so heals it, which lay dead and secure in the world. But while the mind pants after God and despises all worldly things, at once all things are turned into temptation for it and afflict it; but while it is worn by passing labour it is freed from lasting labour. And so he adds:
25_interl2087: by six he understands all the evils of the present world, which runs its course in the six days assigned to work
25_marg768: In six troubles he shall deliver thee, and in the seventh: the number six, which the seventh follows, signifies the work and course of the present life, because on the sixth day God, completing all things, made man, “and on the seventh he rested,” which has no evening, that is, no end. So he delivers in the seventh trouble, so that in the seventh evil may not touch; because here he wears down in fatherly teaching, but on the day of judgment hides from the lash.
25_interl2089: even then he breathes into his faithful, without sound, what is to be done
25_marg769: In famine: he counts up the evils of the present life and the helps of God. The famine of the mind is the silence of the word of God; when this is withdrawn, the temptation of the flesh, which is the battle, grows strong. But God, even in famine, snatches the soul from death, because he refreshes it with his word.
25_interl2090: in the temptation of the flesh
25_marg770: And in battle: he makes them strong against the temptations of the flesh. But one so made sometimes fears detraction. Whence he adds:
25_interl2091: from the word of detraction or insult
25_marg771: From the scourge of the tongue: that is, from the reproach of insult, for which a man, mocked, ceases from good. Whence David: “and from the sharp word.” From this the holy man is hidden, because while he does not seek praise here, neither does he feel insults. But because after these someone fears the tortures of the body, it follows:
25_marg772: And thou shalt not fear calamity, of persecution. But because such a man prepares for himself security in the terror of the judgment to come, he adds:
25_marg773: In destruction and famine: the destruction is hell, which torments without; the famine is hunger, because they will be separated from the sight of the eternal bread. As they sinned within and without, so they will be punished within and without. Or “from the scourge of the tongue,” that is, from the sentence of eternal damnation, which is: “Depart, you cursed, into everlasting fire.” And the just man will be hidden from the calamity that comes, because in that strictness he will be comforted with the gentle voice: “I was hungry, and you gave me to eat”; and he will laugh, cheerful from glory, no longer suffering with the damned, clinging to divine justice by sight; and it would be a lessening of beatitude if he wished anything he could not fulfil. But because here he tastes the beginnings of the security to come, so that he may not fear the old enemy, so that he may not shudder at his assault in the moment of death, he adds:
25_interl2096: at the going out of the present life
25_marg774: And the beasts of the earth, which at the time of death are let loose to snatch souls; but he who did not follow them when they flattered does not fear them when they rage; and the beginning of reward is security of mind at death. But when one lives well, he must take care not to glory in being singular, despising others, but to think again of the common good. Whence he adds:
25_interl2097: with the elect of the Church
25_marg775: But thou shalt have a covenant with the stones of the lands: the lands are, as it were, the divided nations of the Church, differing in customs and language. The stones are the elect, who are set in the building. So he who lives rightly joins himself to the stones by a covenant, because in forsaking the world he binds himself to the saints by imitation; whence the attack grows, by which, however, worn down, he is more humbly subject to God. Whence he adds:
25_interl2100: evil spirits will not attack you
25_marg776: And the beasts of the earth: not ‘at peace’ but ‘peacemaking,’ because they do not have peace but make peace; because the more fiercely a man is attacked by the devil, the more he is driven to love, and a firmer peace is made with God. Or the beasts are the motions of the flesh, which, pressed down by continence as in a cage, even if they roar in tempting, yet do not break out into the deed, as into the frenzy of biting; in this they are peacemaking. Or, because they disturb, that place where one lives with no contradiction is loved the more, and so they drive to the love of inmost quiet.
25_marg777: And thou shalt know that thy tabernacle is in peace, etc. Peace is either begun, which is conceived here from the longing for God, or full, which will be in the future from the sight of God. So when the mind is subjected to God, or the flesh to the mind, the tabernacle of the just man, that is, the body which the mind inhabits, has peace, the motions of the desires being reined in under justice. But this chastity of the flesh is nothing if gentleness of mind in the love of neighbour is not present. Whence he adds:
25_marg778: And visiting thy beauty thou shalt not sin: our beauty is our neighbour, in whom we see what we are; he visits him who goes to him with the steps of love, and, having looked at himself, comes down to him. And this is the tree that brings forth seed after its kind, that is, the mind which considers another from itself and brings forth the shoot of right work. Behold Paul, who comes near to all, coming down to them indeed but not falling. And he fully conquers sin who weighs from himself how he may be widened in love of his neighbour. But when the flesh is restrained and the mind exercised in virtues, it remains that he teach by speaking the life he keeps in his conduct, because from the seed of good work he gathers rich fruits of preaching. Whence he adds:
25_marg779: Thou shalt know also that thy seed shall be multiplied: for he receives the gift of speaking well who lives well, and his conscience does not hinder him as he speaks. Hence it is that the Egyptians, made slaves, receive corn for seed, who, while free before, had received it for eating; because when we are fully subject to God we are filled with the word of preaching. Before, as free men, we are fed with the sacred word, and yet are taken up with some things we seek in the world. From preaching follows a great offspring of the faithful. And this is:
25_marg780: And thy offspring like the grass of the earth: that is, countless. Or it is compared to grass because, forsaking the withering glory of the world, it grows green with inward hope. But it is not enough for the just man to do these great things outwardly unless he also penetrates to eternal things by contemplation. Whence he adds:
25_marg781: Thou shalt enter into the grave in abundance: the grave is contemplation, which hides in its inmost places those dead to the world; and the active life in a way buries, covering those dead to wicked ways. But contemplation buries more perfectly in abundance, because it has first gathered the works of the active life. He is not a perfect preacher who puts works after contemplation, or contemplation after works. Whence Christ, the pattern of life, works miracles in the cities by day and prays through the night on the mountains. Those who contemplate, fixed in the love of God, drink in what they pour out for the good of their neighbours.
25_marg782: As a heap of wheat is brought: because the time of action comes first, of contemplation last. And the perfect man must first exercise his mind in virtues, and afterwards store it in the barn of quiet. Or the grave is eternal rest, in which one rests the more truly the more perfectly the life of corruption is put to death. He enters it in abundance who, after gathering the works of this life, wholly dead to this changeableness, is hidden in the secret place of the true light, like wheat. Because the just feel persecutions in a time not their own, but in their own they go in like grain into the barn.
25_interl2102: as if: I have not lied
25_marg783: As we have searched out: by this he notes that he spoke above of the grave, the beasts, the stones, the tabernacle and suchlike not according to the surface, but sought the inner things in them.
25_marg784: Which thou having heard: words of boasting. Even if he taught well, it is unskilful to want to teach a better man; whence the sayings of the friends, even if right, are reproved as not rightly said.
